title: Driver OOM -> Kernel Panic investigation log & runbook sketch
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from an on-call chain that tied a user-visible kernel panic back to a sequence where the NVIDIA driver hit an internal OOM while handling large KV cache allocations during long-running inference sessions. This doc is a working investigation log plus a compact runbook sketch intended for nightshift engineers. Not final; lots of unresolved hypotheses and TODOs.

Symptoms observed:
- Customer calls: 3 separate Dedicated hosts experienced hard kernel panics with no graceful crash.
- Node state: irrecoverable until manual power-cycle.
- Preceding signs (from node telemetry): rising GPU mem usage, long-running CUDA contexts, intermittent driver WARN logs ~45s before panic.
- Notable: dmesg snippets show driver OOM followed by watchdog/kernel panic stack.

Representative logs (redacted):
[  1423.412345] NVRM: GPU memory allocation failed: os_alloc failed size=0x5a00000
[  1423.412367] nvidia: GPU[0]: internal OOM while allocating KV cache region
[  1423.412389] kernel: BUG: unable to handle kernel paging request at ffffffffdeadbeef
[  1423.412401] kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception in interrupt

Initial hypothesis / causal chain (working):
1) Long-lived inference sessions with high prefix lengths request large KV cache allocations or trigger cache growth paths in runtime.
2) The NVIDIA driver tries to allocate contiguous GPU memory or locked host pages and fails (internal OOM).
3) Driver doesn't safely surface failure to userspace; it triggers a sequence where a callback runs in interrupt context and dereferences a NULL/invalid pointer -> kernel panic.

Why this is plausible:
- We saw kernel backtraces that unwind into driver callback handlers rather than user process context.
- Multiple different models (not a single model) implicated, suggests resource behaviour rather than model-level bug.
- Pattern repeats after sustained traffic burst on the host; not single-request fluke.

Repro attempts so far:
- Local lab repro: ran a stress harness that allocates and frees large KV caches with synthetic prefixes; intermittent OOM observed on older driver build (510-ish family), kernel panic did not always reproduce, but we could force driver OOM with tuned allocation size.
- Tested on newer driver candidate r: driver-patches#34 (linked above) which returns an allocation error gracefully in the harness, but the production fleet still shows panic events on that release in limited cases. Need more lab parity (same kernel + firmware + BIOS).

Immediate on-call triage checklist (fast):
1) If node is still alive: SSH and collect dmesg | tail -n 200, journalctl -k --since "10m ago".
2) Pull driver logs: /var/log/nvidia-installer.log, and driver module messages (modinfo nvidia; lsmod | grep nvidia).
3) Check CUDA contexts and processes: nvidia-smi pmon -c 1; nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,name,used_gpu_memory --format=csv -l 1  (capture several seconds).
4) If memory usage trending upward across GPUs for >30s under steady load, consider evicting the heaviest process (kill -9 <pid>) as a temporary mitigation; note: this can cause inference errors upstream.
5) If node already panicked: mark node out of rotation, preserve core dump artifacts (if crash kernel configured), tag host in inventory with 'panic-driver-oom' and attach collected logs to JIRA ticket.

Short-term mitigations (stopgap):
- Add a transient autoscaler/policy tweak: when average GPU mem usage > 85% for 60s, route new requests away from node (reduce scheduling pressure).
- On Dedicated pools, enable soft-oom monitoring that kills the top memory consumer if we detect the kernel OOM pattern (dangerous but preferable to a full host panic). This should be behind a feature flag.
- Recommend rolling rollback of the driver candidate on hosts where panic frequency increased after driver upgrade.

Instrumentation and telemetry we need (actionable):
- Capture driver internal OOM counters per host (new metric: nvidia.driver.internal_oom_count).
- Expose KV cache allocation growth traces aggregated by model and route.
- Histogram of allocation sizes that fail on driver side (size buckets).
- Correlate kernel panic timestamps with recent driver WARN/ERR messages and with nvidia-smi memory samples from the minute preceding the crash.

Runbook sketch for after-hours engineer (concise):
- Step A (alive + high memory): ssh -> sudo journalctl -k -b -1 | grep -i nvrm; grab last 200 lines of dmesg -> upload to ticket.
- Step B (identify culprit): nvidia-smi pmon and top-like sampling; if single process >70% of GPU mem and sustained, evict.
- Step C (if driver OOM present): set host to maintenance in fleet manager, add drivers:oom=true tag and escalate to eng-serviceruntime team.
- Step D (if kernel panic already happened): run automated collection job (if available) to fetch vmcore, kernel logs; if no vmcore, collect /var/log/messages, kubelet logs, and last-known nvidia-smi samples.

Open questions / unknowns to investigate:
- Why does the driver transition from returning an allocation error to triggering kernel panic in some cases? Is there a particular callback path that is not checking for NULL?
- Are there firmware/BIOS/CPU interplay conditions that make allocation paths more fragile? (observed correlation with a specific BIOS revision on ~6 hosts)
- Is host memory pressure (hugepages, pinned host pages) contributing to failure to back GPU allocations?
- Could aggressive paging/hugepage defrag at OS level reduce occurrences?

Proposed longer-term engineering workstreams:
1) Driver patch upstream: ensure all allocation failure paths return errors gracefully and never dereference driver allocation pointers in interrupt context. Owner: firmware/driver eng (linked PR above).
2) Runtime defensive changes: runtime should detect driver OOM responses and fail requests gracefully rather than retrying allocation-heavy paths. Owner: serving-runtime team.
3) Fleet policy: add preflight checks for driver/farm parity (kernel, driver, BIOS combos known-good matrix). Owner: platform-engineering.
4) Telemetry: expose more granular allocation telemetry + alert when allocation failure rates spike. Owner: observability team.

Action items (tracked):
- [ ] Capture full vmcore from 2 affected hosts (Aisha)
- [ ] Add internal_oom_count metric to driver exporter (Marco)
- [ ] Add runbook as short play to oncall rotation handbook (SRE docs) (Sofia)
- [ ] Coordinate driver rollback for hosts that regressed post-upgrade (Ben)
- [ ] Schedule cross-team incident review next week (invite: eng-serving-runtime, firmware, platform-eng)

Notes to self / rapid scribbles:
- When repro harness toggles allocation granularity down to <1MB chunks, driver returns errors cleanly in lab. Panic seems tied to mid-sized allocations ~5-60MB that likely use different allocation route.
- Check whether HMM (heterogeneous memory management) hooks differ between kernels (5.x vs 6.x) we run in prod.
- Consider adding a per-host mitigation that pre-emptively restarts GPU driver at 03:30 local if internal_oom_count > 10 in last 12h (reduces cumulative leak-like behaviour).

If you pick this up on nightshift: tag the ticket JIRA-OPS-1127 and add a short summary to slack thread #sre-gpu with the phrase: "driver-oom-panic-handback" so we can find events in the morning.

End of draft.
next_steps: Add driver internal OOM metric to exporter
Draft defensive runtime changes for allocation failure handling
Schedule incident review with firmware and runtime teams
